title: Non-surgical rescue oxygenation for otherwise unmanageable airways

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a non-surgical rescue system that maintains adequate gas exchange when existing non-surgical airway methods cannot do so. Although the title emphasizes oxygenation, the intended capability includes both supplying oxygen and clearing carbon dioxide. It would provide a temporary means of sustaining a patient through an otherwise unmanageable airway emergency; no specific device, route of delivery, or physiological mechanism is established in the supplied material.

The concept encompasses failure scenarios involving anatomical obstruction, blood or vomit, swelling, trauma, and equipment or operator limitations. These are proposed operating challenges, not demonstrated capabilities. A system that works in one such situation cannot be assumed to work in the others, and success across every anatomy or injury is not a reasonable requirement.

significance.text: As a conditional impact assessment, promptly and safely restoring adequate gas exchange could prevent some deaths and hypoxic brain injuries during airway emergencies. The consequential advance would be effective rescue in clinically important situations where available non-surgical methods have failed. Merely offering another way to deliver oxygen would not meet the full goal if carbon dioxide accumulated or adequate gas exchange could not be sustained.

A further conditional benefit would be rescue by less-specialized responders or in settings without immediate surgical expertise. That possibility requires separate evidence about usability, training, equipment, deployment time, and recognition of failure. Success in expert hands would establish neither reliable field use nor suitability for responders with less experience.

The potential impact remains bounded by the system's eventual mechanism, rescue duration, injury risks, and failure conditions. A useful system might provide time for definitive treatment or reduce the need for invasive rescue in selected cases, but those are downstream possibilities rather than demonstrated outcomes. Neither technical feasibility nor the number of preventable deaths or injuries can be determined from the supplied evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is a practical, non-surgical means of sustaining both oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide removal after conventional non-surgical airway management has failed. The proposal does not identify how gas exchange would continue despite the particular obstruction or ventilation failure. Selecting and validating a mechanism is therefore a foundational research question, rather than an implementation detail already resolved.

Proposed engineering barriers include maintaining performance despite restricted anatomy, swelling, disrupted tissue, and contamination with blood or vomit. Different causes of failure may demand different solutions: overcoming a passage obstruction does not by itself establish performance in a contaminated airway or under a separate cause of ventilation failure. The supplied material provides no experiments showing which of these challenges a single approach could address.

Additional proposed requirements are sufficiently rapid deployment, sustained gas exchange for a useful rescue interval, acceptable injury risk, and clear identification of situations in which the method will fail. A clinically credible design would also need a safe transition to the next rescue option. For use beyond specialist teams, performance under realistic equipment and operator constraints would be an additional breakthrough requirement.

current_state.text: The reconciled research identifies a Canadian Airway Focus Group consensus publication by Law and colleagues, reported as published online on 18 June 2021 in the Canadian Journal of Anesthesia, DOI 10.1007/s12630-021-02007-0. The research reports that its abstract describes difficult-airway management pathways and recommends prompt emergency front-of-neck access when ventilation remains impossible. It also characterizes the recommendations as combining evidence and expert consensus. These are attributed descriptions from the supplied research; the retained evidence available to the review did not independently verify the publication's identity or recommendation content.

There is a material access limitation. Although the research says the abstract was inspected, the review found only a cookie-access notice in the retained HTML, with no readable abstract or recommendations. The source index records a saved artifact retrieved on 11 November 2026, containing 153 extracted characters, and marks it verified with no extraction issues. Those metadata do not resolve the review's finding that substantive article content was unavailable. The retained artifact therefore cannot substantiate the clinical recommendations attributed to the paper, but this extraction failure is not evidence that those recommendations are false.

If the recommendation is accurately represented in the research, it illustrates the continuing role of an invasive rescue option when ventilation cannot be restored. It does not establish that a broadly effective non-surgical replacement is technically feasible. This is a logical distinction between identifying an unmet need and demonstrating a solution; the cited recommendation itself remains unverified in the retained material.

The supplied materials document no prototype, bench result, animal study, clinical demonstration, rescue duration, gas-exchange measurement, or quantified patient benefit for this proposed innovation. No preprint or disputed experimental result is supplied for assessment. The bounded search record is empty, so the materials also do not establish the field's state as of 1 November 2026. These are limits of the available record, not a finding that no relevant technology or research exists.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: begin with bench and large-animal testing across predefined, clinically relevant conditions, including severe obstruction, airway contamination, varied anatomy, and ventilation failure. Tests should measure oxygenation, carbon dioxide clearance, time to rescue, the duration for which adequate gas exchange is sustained, and injury. Results should be reported separately for the different failure scenarios so that aggregate success does not conceal important weaknesses.
completion_criteria.label: Bench and large-animal rescue performance reported separately by failure scenario

completion_criteria.text: Proposed protocol requirements: specify effectiveness and safety thresholds, the intended rescue interval, stopping rules, and criteria for moving to another rescue pathway before testing. The supplied material establishes no numerical thresholds, and these requirements should not be presented as existing clinical standards. A convincing result would show timely, sustained gas exchange with acceptable harm within the system's declared operating conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Timely, sustained gas exchange meets predefined effectiveness and safety thresholds

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical evaluation: after suitable preclinical evidence, carefully governed studies should compare effectiveness, safety, and time to rescue against applicable rescue pathways. Evaluation should establish patient-selection boundaries, training requirements, and recognizable failure conditions. Claims for less-specialized responders or settings without immediate surgical expertise would require direct testing in those intended circumstances.
completion_criteria.label: Clinical studies compare effectiveness, safety, and time to rescue

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirement: independent teams should reproduce performance using sufficiently documented equipment, procedures, operator training, and test conditions. Demonstrated breadth across a finite set of anatomies and emergencies would support a bounded clinical claim, not literal universality. Successful completion need not mean avoiding surgery in every case; it should mean a reproducible, useful rescue capability with explicit limits and a reliable transition when it fails.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams reproduce rescue performance with explicit operating limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: EMR-01, Reversible emergency metabolic suspension, and EMR-02, Neurologically intact recovery after prolonged untreated cardiac arrest, overlap with EMR-08 in their concern with surviving interruptions in oxygen availability. Their proposed capabilities remain distinct: metabolic suspension concerns temporarily reducing physiological demand, recovery after prolonged arrest concerns recovery after an extended untreated event, and EMR-08 concerns maintaining gas exchange during an airway emergency. Success in one would not establish either of the others.

Roster-based synthesis: EMR-03, Field treatment that safely stops inaccessible internal bleeding, and EMR-04, Inexpensive, universally compatible emergency blood replacement, address different threats to oxygen delivery. Bleeding control concerns stopping blood loss, blood replacement concerns replacing lost blood functions, and EMR-08 concerns gas exchange. These capabilities could be complementary in trauma, but airway rescue alone would not establish control of hemorrhage or replacement of blood.

Roster-based synthesis: EMR-05, A portable, broad-spectrum emergency diagnostic system, could overlap with identifying the cause of deterioration and selecting an appropriate rescue pathway. Diagnosis and rescue remain separate capabilities: identifying an airway problem would not itself provide gas exchange, while a rescue system would still require evidence defining when it should be used.

Roster-based synthesis: EMR-06, Rapid reversal of septic shock and its harmful host response, and EMR-07, Broad-spectrum emergency antidote platform, concern underlying systemic or toxic causes of critical illness. EMR-08 could potentially provide supportive gas exchange during such emergencies if its operating conditions allowed, but that would not demonstrate reversal of septic shock, modification of the harmful host response, or neutralization of a toxin.

Roster-based synthesis: EMR-09, Effective early prevention of post-traumatic stress disorder after emergency care, and EMR-10, Rapid, potent non-opioid treatment for severe acute pain, concern psychological and pain outcomes associated with emergency care. They remain separate from the immediate physiological objective of EMR-08. Successful airway rescue would not establish prevention of post-traumatic stress disorder or effective analgesia.

Roster-based synthesis: EMR-11, Acute rescue and repair of injured vital tissue, overlaps with the goal of limiting organ damage. EMR-08 could conditionally help prevent additional injury by sustaining gas exchange, whereas repairing tissue already injured is a separate proposed capability. Prevention of further oxygen-related harm should not be treated as evidence of tissue repair.

unresolved_issues: The article's identity, abstract, and recommendation content remain unverified in the retained evidence; the conflict between reported abstract inspection and the saved access notice is unresolved.
The source index's verified designation and absence of recorded extraction issues do not explain why the review found only an access notice.
No mechanism is specified for maintaining gas exchange despite obstruction, contamination, trauma, or ventilation failure.
The attainable rescue duration, deployment time, effectiveness, injury risk, and anatomical boundaries are unknown.
Numerical success thresholds, stopping rules, and appropriate comparator pathways remain to be defined and justified.
Feasibility for less-specialized responders and settings without immediate surgical expertise remains a separate open question.
The supplied record cannot establish research freshness, current clinical applicability, or the magnitude of potential patient benefit.

brief.title: Rescuing breathing without emergency surgery
possible: A person whose airway cannot be managed with existing non-surgical methods could receive temporary support without an emergency operation. The rescue would keep oxygen entering the blood and carbon dioxide leaving it while the team arranges further treatment.
why: Restoring this exchange quickly could prevent deaths and brain injuries caused by oxygen deprivation. It could buy time for treatment when ordinary airway rescue has failed.
A system that less-specialized responders could use could also bring rescue to settings without immediate surgical expertise.

sources.who: J Adam Law and the Canadian Airway Focus Group
sources.showed: The group combined published evidence and expert consensus into airway management recommendations. It recommends emergency access through the neck when breathing support remains impossible.
sources.quote: Most studies comparing video laryngoscopy (VL) with direct laryngoscopy indicate a higher first attempt and overall success rate with VL, and lower complication rates.
sources.cited_for: The recommendations describe the emergency in which a further non-surgical rescue option would be useful.
sources.not_established: Clinical recommendations do not demonstrate a non-surgical system that can sustain oxygen supply and carbon dioxide removal.

sources.who: Julia Garcia Mancebo, Kristen Sack and colleagues
sources.showed: Tiny oxygen-filled bubbles injected into the bloodstream improved survival and brain and kidney function in pigs after temporary airway blockage.
sources.quote:
We show

neurologic outcomes in a realistic animal model of severe hypoxaemic 
cardiac arrest.
sources.cited_for: Injected oxygen improved outcomes in an animal model of temporary airway blockage.
sources.not_established: The study does not establish carbon dioxide removal or effective rescue in humans.

sources.who: Paul A. Mountford, Premila D. Leiphrakpam and colleagues
sources.showed: Oxygen-filled bubbles delivered into the colon, part of the large intestine, raised blood oxygen and lowered carbon dioxide in a small study of pigs with smoke-damaged lungs.
sources.quote:
resulted in significant improvements in 
systemic oxygenation
sources.cited_for: Delivery through the intestine improved both blood oxygen and carbon dioxide levels in pigs.
sources.not_established: The pigs also received mechanical breathing support; the study does not establish rescue after airway methods fail.

sources.who: Michiel W. P. de Wolf and colleagues
sources.showed: Ventrain, a device that pushes gas in and helps draw it out through a narrow tube, restored oxygen and carbon dioxide levels in six pigs with otherwise blocked airways.
sources.quote: Ventrain provides rapid reoxygenation and effective ventilation through a small-bore AEC in pigs with an obstructed airway.
sources.cited_for: Breathing support through a narrow tube restored oxygen supply and carbon dioxide clearance in an animal obstruction model.
sources.not_established: The experiment depended on a tube already passing the blockage and does not establish rescue when that access is impossible.

sources.showed: Oxygen gas or oxygen-carrying liquid delivered through the rectum improved blood oxygen in animal models of breathing failure. The work also reported survival benefits.
sources.quote:
A rodent and
porcine model study conﬁrmed the tolerable and repeatable features
of an enema-like l-EVA procedure wit h no major signs of complications.
sources.cited_for: Animal experiments demonstrated oxygen delivery through the intestine.
sources.not_established: The work does not establish adequate carbon dioxide removal or rescue in humans with otherwise unmanageable airways.

shown: Animal studies have demonstrated parts of the capability. Garcia Mancebo, Sack and colleagues improved survival after temporary airway blockage by injecting oxygen-filled bubbles. Mountford and colleagues improved oxygen and carbon dioxide levels through intestinal delivery in pigs with smoke-damaged lungs.

De Wolf and colleagues restored both gases to normal levels using Ventrain through a narrow tube in pigs with otherwise blocked airways. These experiments have not established a complete rescue system for humans when existing non-surgical airway methods fail.
missing: A practical system must sustain both oxygen supply and carbon dioxide removal after conventional non-surgical airway rescue fails.
Tests must establish which blockages, injuries, swelling and contamination a system can handle.
Rescue must begin quickly, last long enough and cause acceptable harm, with clear signs for switching to another method.
Clinical studies must establish effectiveness and safety, including direct testing wherever less-specialized responders would use it.

milestones.label: Laboratory and large-animal rescue succeeds across defined emergencies
milestones.explanation: Laboratory and large-animal tests would have to measure both gases, rescue speed, duration and injury separately for each failure scenario. This would reveal useful performance and hidden weaknesses.

milestones.label: Timely rescue meets agreed effectiveness and safety thresholds
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to meet predefined limits for oxygen supply, carbon dioxide removal, rescue duration and harm, with rules for stopping or switching methods. This would establish useful rescue within declared conditions.

milestones.label: Clinical comparisons establish rescue performance and safety
milestones.explanation: Clinical studies would have to compare effectiveness, safety and rescue speed against applicable rescue pathways, defining patient and training limits. Direct testing would establish suitability for intended users and settings.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce rescue within explicit limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce performance with documented equipment, procedures, training and conditions. This would establish reliable rescue with clear limits and a dependable transition when it fails.

uncertain: Which approach can sustain both gases when the airway cannot be used remains open.
Useful rescue duration, acceptable injury risk and justified success thresholds remain undefined.
Whether less-specialized responders can deploy a system reliably under realistic constraints remains unknown.

page.title: Non-surgical rescue oxygenation and carbon dioxide removal
page.definition: A temporary rescue method delivers oxygen to the blood and removes carbon dioxide without surgery or an airway opening through the front of the neck. It works when a face mask, a supraglottic airway seated above the voice box, and available tracheal tubes or catheters cannot sustain gas exchange. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation can support a patient before an anticipated airway obstruction. The rescue problem is establishing gas exchange in time when airway failure is unexpected.

goal.need: In 2008–09, 309 UK hospitals reported 184 major airway complications, including 38 deaths and 18 other cases of permanent harm. These figures cover several causes. When a tube, mask and supraglottic airway all fail to oxygenate an adult, the team must immediately open an airway through the neck. A rescue that acts within minutes could keep the patient alive while the obstruction is treated. Oxygen delivery alone can leave carbon dioxide accumulating even as blood oxygen levels improve.

figures.caption: Major airway complications reported to the Fourth National Audit Project
figures.note: Deaths and permanent harm are outcomes within the reported complications. These are reported events, not estimates of the proposed method's eligible population.

statements.quote: the physiologic endpoints of ventilation and oxygenation are the more important goals.
statements.context: The consensus recommendations identify failure of tracheal intubation, face-mask ventilation and supraglottic-airway ventilation with current or imminent hypoxaemia as a cannot-ventilate, cannot-oxygenate emergency. They recommend immediate emergency front-of-neck access.

statements.body: Dolphys Medical B.V., developer of Ventrain
statements.quote: Ventrain is specifically designed for 'cannot intubate, cannot ventilate' emergencies where conventional ventilation by mask and/or large-bore endotracheal tube cannot be performed.
statements.context: The developer's submission specifies ventilation through a transtracheal catheter. It establishes an emergency gas-exchange goal but does not establish rescue without neck access.

statements.body: Institute of Science Tokyo, enteral-ventilation development team
statements.quote: These findings provide the foundational safety data to advance enteral ventilation as a novel therapeutic strategy for patients with respiratory failure
statements.context: Takanori Takebe describes development following a human study of rectally administered, non-oxygenated perfluorodecalin. The stated goal concerns respiratory failure rather than specifically failed airway management.

statements.body: US Defense Health Agency, Small Business Innovation Research topic DHA231-004
statements.quote: Minimally or Non-invasive Systemic Oxygen Delivery and Carbon Dioxide Removal
statements.context: The topic sought a drug, biologic or device that could exchange both gases without an oxygen-generating system. Its objective did not specify failed airway access.

completion.title: A regulator authorises non-surgical gas-exchange rescue after available airway methods fail.
completion.criterion: A regulator grants marketing authorisation for a method whose indication explicitly covers temporary oxygen delivery and carbon dioxide removal, without surgery or front-of-neck airway access, when available non-surgical airway methods cannot sustain gas exchange. The authorised indication defines eligible emergencies and operating limits. Clearance requiring a transtracheal neck catheter and authorisation for supplemental oxygenation alone do not satisfy this test.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; indication-specific regulatory authorisation is the Atlas's completion test, not a published airway-society target.
completion.basis: No published method-independent standard specifies a deployment time, support duration and targets for both gases in this airway emergency. The Atlas therefore uses the authorised indication. Ventrain’s US clearance specifies transtracheal access. Novalung’s US clearance covers more than six hours of extracorporeal support in adults with acute respiratory or cardiopulmonary failure after other treatments fail. It does not specify immediate rescue after failure of non-surgical airway methods.

milestones.title: Ventrain restores oxygen saturation >95% and arterial CO2 pressure <45 mmHg within 1 minute in pigs.
milestones.criterion: In anaesthetised pigs with the upper airway obstructed except for a 100 cm airway exchange catheter of 3 mm internal diameter, start Ventrain after peripheral oxygen saturation falls below 70%. Within one minute, arterial oxygen saturation must exceed 95% and arterial carbon dioxide pressure must be below 45 mmHg. Continue ventilation for ten minutes.
milestones.set_by: De Wolf and colleagues, experimental protocol published on 28 October 2016; these thresholds were written for Ventrain through an airway-exchange catheter, not for every rescue mechanism.
milestones.threshold_quote: efficient oxygenation (SaO2 > 95%) and ventilation (PaCO2 < 45 mmHg) could be restored within one minute.

milestones.title: At least half a dose cohort retains rectal perfluorodecalin for 60 minutes after receiving ≥95% of the dose.
milestones.criterion: In healthy men aged 20–45 years, evaluate a single rectal dose of non-oxygenated perfluorodecalin at each planned level of 25, 75, 200, 500, 1,000 and 1,500 mL. Tolerability requires administration of at least 95% of the planned dose and retention for 60 minutes by at least 50% of participants, without early termination due to discomfort or serious adverse events.
milestones.set_by: Fujii and colleagues, published protocol for jRCT2052240047; the thresholds apply specifically to intrarectal perfluorodecalin.
milestones.threshold_quote: of ≥95% of the planned PFD dose and the ability of ≥50% of participants to retain the PFD for 60 min

milestones.title: A rescue method demonstrates gas exchange and initial safety in an authorised human feasibility study.
milestones.criterion: In an authorised early feasibility study for the intended rescue use, demonstrate oxygen delivery and carbon dioxide removal in patients and collect initial clinical safety data. Assess gas exchange and adverse events under the study protocol.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 2013 early-feasibility guidance; this is a general device-development stage, not an airway-specific numerical performance standard.
milestones.threshold_quote: proof of principle and initial clinical safety data.

milestones.title: A pivotal study establishes a rescue device's safety and effectiveness for its intended airway emergency.
milestones.criterion: For a device approach, a pivotal clinical investigation meets its protocol’s success criteria and supplies definitive evidence of safety and effectiveness for the specified non-surgical rescue indication, typically in a statistically justified number of participants.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, definition of a pivotal study in its 2013 early-feasibility guidance; the definition is general and does not prescribe a protocol for this proposed indication.
milestones.threshold_quote: definitive evidence of the safety and effectiveness of a device

milestones.title: A lung simulator completes 600 mL breaths through a 100 cm airway exchange catheter.
milestones.criterion: With the upper airway closed, use Ventrain through a 100 cm catheter of 3 mm internal diameter at 15 L/min. Measure inspiration and expiration times for 600 mL breaths with assisted and passive expiration. Calculate minute volume from five consecutive breaths at each of the six resistance and compliance settings.
milestones.set_by: Dias and colleagues, lung-simulator protocol for expiratory ventilation assistance, 2012.
milestones.threshold_quote: with tidal volumes of 600 ml at variable compliances

milestones.title: Colonic oxygen microbubbles raise arterial oxygen and lower carbon dioxide in smoke-injured pigs.
milestones.criterion: In pigs with severe hypoxia 48 hours after smoke inhalation, compare colonic oxygen microbubbles at 75–100 mL/kg with no treatment. Compare changes from baseline in arterial oxygen and carbon dioxide partial pressures over 150 minutes in six animals per group. The test is an increase in oxygen and a decrease in carbon dioxide relative to controls.
milestones.set_by: Mountford and colleagues, porcine smoke-inhalation study protocol, 2023.
milestones.threshold_quote: significantly increase systemic oxygen levels and reduce systemic carbon dioxide levels in a large-animal model of severe hypoxia.

milestones.title: A near-final rescue device yields preliminary safety and effectiveness data for pivotal trial design.
milestones.criterion: In a traditional feasibility study of a near-final or final rescue device, collect preliminary clinical safety and effectiveness data for its intended use sufficient to plan the pivotal investigation.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 2013 early feasibility guidance, definition of a traditional feasibility study.
milestones.threshold_quote: capture preliminary safety and effectiveness information on a near-final or final device design

not_found: No academy, professional society, government programme or prize statement explicitly setting the entire combined non-surgical replacement capability as a goal was located.
No registered pivotal study defining success thresholds for the full rescue indication was located.
No published authorisation was found that explicitly covers both gas transfers without surgery or front-of-neck access after non-surgical airway rescue fails.

Continue ventilation for ten minutes."; threshold_quote = "efficient oxygenation (SaO2 > 95%) and ventilation (PaCO2 < 45 mmHg) could be restored within one minute."; threshold_ref = 6; refs = [6]. Reason: The existing Ventrain endpoint can retain its result history once the unrelated intestinal experiment and the observed outcomes are removed from its criterion.

add milestone after m1: "Colonic oxygen microbubbles raise arterial oxygen and lower carbon dioxide in smoke-injured pigs.". Reason: The colonic microbubble experiment tests both gases in smoke-injured lungs against untreated controls and needs its own endpoint.

edit m2: title = "At least half a dose cohort retains rectal perfluorodecalin for 60 minutes after receiving \u226595% of the dose."; criterion = "In healthy men aged 20\u201345 years, evaluate a single rectal dose of non-oxygenated perfluorodecalin at each planned level of 25, 75, 200, 500, 1,000 and 1,500 mL. Tolerability requires administration of at least 95% of the planned dose and retention for 60 minutes by at least 50% of participants, without early termination due to discomfort or serious adverse events."; threshold_quote = "of \u226595% of the planned PFD dose and the ability of \u226550% of participants to retain the PFD for 60 min"; threshold_ref = 8; refs = [8, 18]. Reason: The volunteer criterion mixes a dose-retention test with observed adverse events and omits the accessible registry record.

edit m3: criterion = "In an authorised early feasibility study for the intended rescue use, demonstrate oxygen delivery and carbon dioxide removal in patients and collect initial clinical safety data. Assess gas exchange and adverse events under the study protocol."; refs = [9]. Reason: An individual rescue case is clinical evidence but cannot define the success criterion for an authorised early feasibility study.

add milestone after m3: "A near-final rescue device yields preliminary safety and effectiveness data for pivotal trial design.". Reason: FDA guidance distinguishes a feasibility study of a near-final design from initial proof of principle and pivotal testing.

edit m4: criterion = "For a device approach, a pivotal clinical investigation meets its protocol\u2019s success criteria and supplies definitive evidence of safety and effectiveness for the specified non-surgical rescue indication, typically in a statistically justified number of participants.". Reason: The pivotal criterion ends with a search finding that belongs in the entry’s evidence gaps.

structure = parallel. Reason: Catheter ventilation and intestinal gas exchange have independent experimental milestones, and the FDA allows a device to enter a pivotal trial without either feasibility stage.
